pulses.summary: Mostly vendor studies of medium or low confidence, and few used B2B SaaS data. The only firm news is Google's September spam update (rolling out now) and ChatGPT Ads opening to self-service in Europe.

points.text: Google's September 2026 spam update started on 24 Sep and can take up to two weeks to roll out. Log traffic changes against that window and hold off on big content changes until it ends. Google hasn't said which spam types it targets, so don't diagnose drops yet.

AI referrals convert well but are tiny. Orbit's 29M-visit dataset shows AI visitors are 3x more likely to become leads, yet AI is only 0.5% of traffic. This is medium confidence, and AI traffic is undercounted because AI Overviews and AI Mode land in Organic Search. Track AI referrals as a high-intent channel, but don't move budget away from organic search. Semrush's manufacturing study adds that mentions, citations and referral traffic don't move together, so measure them separately.

Single-run AI visibility numbers are unreliable. Orbit's sample is very small (three brands, low confidence) and found the four LLMs almost never cited the same domain. Profound's persona tests were consumer-only and medium confidence, but they also showed answers shifting a lot. Use repeated runs across engines, and test your key prompts with buyer role context, before trusting any score.

briefs.title: Announcing web multimodal Search performance reporting in Search Console  |  Google Search Central Blog  |  Google for Developers

brief.headline: Google added a "multimodal" search type filter to Search Console's Performance and Generative AI features reports, covering image-based searches such as Lens and Circle to Search.
key_stats: Covers searches with Lens, Circle to Search on Android, image uploads to Google Search, and Chrome right-click "Search this image"
Appears in both the Search results performance report and the Generative AI features report, via a new multimodal search type filter
Rolling out globally starting September 24, 2026; data can be exported

method.sample: n/a (official announcement)
method.data_source: n/a (official announcement)
method.timeframe: Rolling out globally starting 2026-09-24. Metrics appear if a site receives traffic from these queries.
method.conflict: Google does not say how much multimodal traffic exists, how it is counted, or how impressions and clicks are attributed. It also gives no optimization guidance and does not say whether the Generative AI report is separate from standard Web data.
method.caveat: The post has no volume figures, metric definitions or historical backfill details. It also doesn't say whether B2B SaaS sites will see meaningful multimodal traffic.

brief.why_it_matters: You can now measure image-initiated search visibility, including in the AI features report. Check the filter for your site before deciding whether visual content deserves any investment.

briefs.title: ChatGPT Ads expands across Europe

brief.headline: OpenAI is bringing ChatGPT Ads to 31 European markets, including Germany, France, Spain and Italy, with self-service access via Ads Manager now live.
key_stats: Expansion to 31 European markets; largest to date, after a U.S. pilot in February and eight additional markets
Ads shown only to Free and Go plan users; Plus, Pro and Enterprise stay ad-free
Tens of thousands of marketers have advertised; new bidding beyond CPM/CPC (conversion optimization), geo-targeting, custom audiences, OpenAI Pixel and Conversions API

method.sample: n/a (official announcement)
method.data_source: n/a (official announcement)
method.timeframe: Announced August 18, 2026; rollout the following week via OpenAI Ads Solutions team, agencies and tech partners. Update of August 31, 2026: self-service via Ads Manager available in all 31 markets.
method.conflict: OpenAI does not publish any performance data (CTR, conversion, CPM/CPC pricing), ad formats, placement rules or how ads are matched to conversations. It also does not name all 31 markets, and its claim that ads do not influence answers is unverified.
method.caveat: The rollout facts are specific and dated, but the post gives no results, pricing, formats or targeting detail, so it cannot show whether the ads work for B2B SaaS.

brief.why_it_matters: Paid placement in ChatGPT is now open to self-service in Europe, so you can test it for software-comparison queries. Organic GEO work still cannot buy answer placement, since OpenAI says ads do not influence answers.

briefs.title: Do Answer Engines customize responses to different personas?

brief.headline: Answer engines change brand recommendations by persona: different personas asking the same prompt shared about 1 in 4 brand mentions and 20% of cited domains, versus about 2 in 5 brands for repeat runs of one persona.
key_stats: Brand overlap: same persona about 2 in 5, different personas about 1 in 4 (15-point drop); cited domain overlap 34% vs 20%
High-income personas averaged 7.5 brand mentions and 4.8 citations vs 5.8 and 4.1 for low-income
Clothing queries for people in their 50s and 70s were about 39 percentage points more likely to contain "women" than queries for younger age groups

method.sample: 71,147 responses from ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, using base prompts from three Profound Index categories: credit card, clothing, furniture. Prompts were varied by gender, age, income or occupation.
method.data_source: Profound's own prompt runs on ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. Search queries were recorded for ChatGPT and Claude only.
method.timeframe: 14 days, August 11–24, 2026
method.conflict: Yes. Profound sells AI visibility tracking, and the article ends with a demo pitch for persona-level tracking, which is the article's main recommendation.
method.caveat: The tests covered only consumer categories (clothing, furniture, credit cards), used a one-line "I am [attribute]" prefix, and covered one two-week window. None of this is B2B SaaS, and real users rarely state their persona so bluntly. The article also gives no significance testing, no prompt counts per category and no per-engine breakdown for most results.

brief.why_it_matters: Aggregate AI visibility scores can hide gaps for your target buyer. It is worth testing your key prompts with role and budget context, but these consumer results may not carry over to B2B software.

briefs.title: AI search & manufacturing SEO: What the data shows [Study]

brief.headline: Google AI Overviews reached 57% of tracked manufacturing search volume in July 2026, up from 38% in January, while AI sources drove just 0.48% of sessions.
key_stats: AI Overviews: 38% of search volume (Jan 2026) to 57% (July), across 458 manufacturing keywords
0.48% of all sessions to manufacturing sites come from AI search tools or assistants
Only two domains (Vevor, Grainger) appear on both the top 15 most-mentioned and top 15 most-cited lists

method.sample: 458 manufacturing keywords; US clickstream sessions across ten manufacturing categories; top 25 domains per month by mentions and by citations across four LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, AI Mode, AI Overviews). Number of domains in clickstream set not disclosed.
method.data_source: Semrush's own datasets: keyword/SERP snapshots, clickstream, AI Visibility database, Traffic and Market Toolkit.
method.timeframe: January to July 2026
method.conflict: Yes, it is Semrush's own tools and data, and it recommends monitoring AI visibility, which its products sell. The promotion is mild.
method.caveat: The keyword set was built from the top 20 domains in Semrush's own ranking, and the authors call the results directional. Explanations for the traffic gaps, such as engineerfix's generic content, are interpretation from a handful of domains, not tested.

brief.why_it_matters: For a B2B SaaS lead, this is a manufacturing-sector study, so treat it as an analogue. Its main lesson carries over: mentions and citations are separate metrics that don't reliably predict AI referral traffic, so track them separately.

briefs.title: AI chatbots talked 57.5% of AI users out of buying

brief.headline: In a survey of 2,338 US adults, 57.5% of AI users say an AI chatbot has led them to decide not to buy something.
key_stats: 57.51% of AI users have bought a product on an AI recommendation, and 57.5% have decided against a purchase on chatbot information
74.15% of all consumers would be at least somewhat less likely to buy if a chatbot flagged mixed or negative reviews
23.12% would think worse of a product after seeing an AI chatbot ad, against 20.36% who would think better

method.sample: 2,338 US adults, at least 300 per age band. Margin of error ±2 percentage points for the full sample, wider for filtered segments.
method.data_source: Exploding Topics consumer survey, published on the Semrush blog. Panel provider and recruitment method not disclosed. Answers are self-reported.
method.timeframe: July 2026
method.conflict: Yes. The article ends by calling Semrush Enterprise AIO and the AI Visibility Toolkit the best GEO tools, and it frames the findings as proof that GEO is essential.
method.caveat: The figures are self-reported consumer attitudes, not observed behavior. Many stats use different, smaller filtered subsets, and the sample is general US consumers rather than B2B software buyers.

brief.why_it_matters: It adds survey evidence that what chatbots say about your brand, including negative reviews, can block a sale. It also suggests AI ads may not pay off for B2B, since ChatGPT Plus, Pro and business plans are ad-free.

briefs.title: ChatGPT 5.6 has transformed Shopping mode

brief.headline: Profound reports ChatGPT Shopping shifted from web search to feed-integrated retrieval on July 10th, rising from 8.26% to 61.54% in one day after GPT 5.6 launched.
key_stats: Feed-integrated retrieval rose from 8.26% to 61.54% on July 10th; brands not integrated are excluded from ~65% of Shopping recommendations
Top 10 merchant share rose from 22.5% to 41.8%; unique merchants fell from 13,524 to 10,607 (Jul 7-9 vs Jul 10-12)
Shopify is ~35% of feed-integrated retrieval; 517 customers with ≥33% visibility swings, joint model explains 83% of the swings

method.sample: 687 Profound customers analysed, narrowed to 517 with ≥33% visibility swings. Prompt runs range from 33,167 to 1,757,723 depending on the section, with 10% to 100% sampling.
method.data_source: Profound's own Shopping-mode prompt tracking data from its customers
method.timeframe: July 1 to Aug 24, 2026 (the main swing analysis covers July 7-12)
method.conflict: Yes. Profound sells Shopping visibility tracking, and the call to action (get feed-integrated) fits its product category. It does not name a Profound product in the recommendation.
method.caveat: The GPT 5.6 cause is inferred from timing alone, and the customers were picked because they had big swings. The 83% figure is therefore not a general effect. The merchant consolidation comparison covers only two 3-day windows.

brief.why_it_matters: This matters only if you sell physical products through ChatGPT Shopping. For a B2B SaaS team it has little direct use, though it shows how fast AI retrieval sources can change.

briefs.title: Study: AI Declined to Answer Prompts About Our Brand 31% of the Time (But Got Our Info Mostly Right When It Answered)

brief.headline: Across six AI platforms, Seer Interactive got branded answers right 95.9% of the time when they answered, but they declined 31.2% of the time.
key_stats: Average inaccurate response rate 2.8%; average no-answer rate 31.2%; total accurate rate 66%
Comparative prompts: 18.8% accurate, 80.3% no answer. Direct prompts 90.4% accurate, indirect 88.7%
Claude: 98% accurate when it answered, but 46.3% no-answer rate, so total accuracy was 52.6%

method.sample: 1,562 branded prompts, 28,123 AI responses, 87 brand attributes, 6 platforms (AI Mode, AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity). One brand only: Seer Interactive.
method.data_source: Seer's own daily prompt tracking, apparently through Scrunch (named as the data set). How responses were scored as accurate or inaccurate is not explained.
method.timeframe: May 1 to June 9, 2026 (about 5 weeks)
method.conflict: Yes. Seer sells AI visibility and brand canon services, and the article ends with a sales call to action for both.
method.caveat: The data covers one agency's brand, and Seer graded accuracy against its own brand canon without explaining how, so the rates may not carry over to a B2B SaaS brand. The "fix timelines" are asserted without supporting data.

brief.why_it_matters: Brand misinformation matters less than absence. Comparative prompts returned no answer 80.3% of the time, so third-party coverage is the bigger gap. The fact-versus-narrative and importance grid is a usable way to triage errors.

briefs.title: Analysis: Reddit Appears in 83.9% of Google's Discussions and Forums Results

brief.headline: Reddit appears in 83.9% of Google's 'Discussions and forums' results worldwide, and Reddit, Facebook and Quora together take 76.75% of all links in the feature.
key_stats: Feature present in 16.93M (11.7%) of 145M US Google results; Reddit in 87.8% of US SERPs (83.9% worldwide)
After Reddit: Facebook 38.3%, Quora 32%, JustAnswer 8.2%, Mayo Clinic 3.3%
98.7% of appearances are informational intent (40.9% commercial); 43.2% are for queries of 5+ words

method.sample: 145M US Google search results, with the feature in 16.93M of them. Also dozens of countries and the top 1,000 domains. The worldwide sample size is not disclosed.
method.data_source: Ahrefs' own SERP and keyword data. The domain age checks used registration dates and archive.org.
method.timeframe: Not disclosed for the main dataset. Reddit's 89.3% average inclusion rate covers the past two years, and August 2026 data was still being collected.
method.conflict: Partly. The article ends by pointing readers to Ahrefs Keywords Explorer and Brand Radar. The core Reddit finding does not depend on the product.
method.caveat: This is vendor data with no keyword-set or collection method explained. Reddit's share appears as 83.9%, 84.71% (table) and 87.8% (US), and the article does not explain the differences. It also claims Facebook's share is identical in every country, which is unusual and not explained.

brief.why_it_matters: The feature shows on only about 1 in 9 US SERPs, and Reddit, Facebook and Quora dominate it. For B2B SaaS, the practical route in is participating in those communities, not building your own forum. Backlinks to individual threads showed no correlation with appearances.

briefs.title: Claude and Claude Code are distinct Answer Engines

brief.headline: Claude Code searched the web in 13% of responses versus 93% for Claude, and the two mentioned the same brands only 20% of the time on average.
key_stats: Claude Code searches in 13% of responses vs Claude's 93%; brand overlap between the two averages 20%
Nearly three-quarters of Claude Code agent visits went to documentation, informational and pricing pages vs 5% for Claude's agent
60% of Claude agent visits went to robots.txt, sitemaps and home pages vs 4% for Claude Code's agent

method.sample: 24,135 responses across 1,724 prompts from 11 randomly sampled categories (coding subset: 2,800 responses, 200 prompts); plus the top 1,000 pages visited by each agent
method.data_source: Profound's own prompt runs with web search enabled, and Profound's internally tracked domains for agent visits. Pages were scraped with Firecrawl and categorized by an LLM (gpt-4.1-mini).
method.timeframe: Prompts run 07/13/2026 to 07/23/2026; agent page visits July 18 to August 18, 2026
method.conflict: Yes. Profound sells AI answer-engine visibility tracking, and the article argues that Claude Code must be measured as a separate engine, then ends with a demo pitch.
method.caveat: The agent-visit data covers only Profound's tracked domains, which aren't described. It counts visits to the top 1,000 pages, not real users, and an LLM classified the page types, so the "optimize docs and pricing pages" advice is an inference rather than a tested result.

brief.why_it_matters: If your buyers are developers, Claude Code may read your docs and pricing pages rather than search the web. Keep those pages specific and current, and don't assume Claude results predict Claude Code results.

briefs.title: Where do inaccurate AI claims come from?

brief.headline: In 158,000+ analyzed claims, inaccurate AI claims came mostly from competitor and earned media sources, and pricing and billing was 12% of evaluated claims but 24% of inaccurate ones.
key_stats: Pricing and billing: 12% of evaluated claims but 24% of all inaccurate claims; next largest, eligibility and terms, 4%
51% of brands had at least one inaccurate claim citing earned media; 54% had one citing their own content
Inaccuracy rates by Answer Engine range from 4.3-6.8%; Claude is more than 1.3 times more inaccurate than ChatGPT

method.sample: Over 158,000 claims in FactCheck data; number of brands, prompts and industries not disclosed
method.data_source: Profound's own FactCheck product data, with claims judged accurate or inaccurate against brand records. How verdicts were reached is not explained.
method.timeframe: Snapshot of the most recently completed FactCheck run as of August 14, 2026
method.conflict: Yes. Profound sells FactCheck, and the research promotes it and the case for ongoing monitoring of AI claims.
method.caveat: The data comes from the vendor's own new tool, and the article does not say how claims were verified, how many brands were covered, or which models were tested. It admits the pricing result may partly reflect a selection effect, and the results are observational.

brief.why_it_matters: It suggests checking pricing and billing details first, on your own site and on third-party pages. The evidence is vendor data, so treat it as a lead to test, not a proven ranking.

briefs.title: AI Citations Aren't Your Top KPI: ChatGPT-5.6 Luna Runs More Targeted Searches

brief.headline: GPT-5.6 Luna used site: operator in 76% of fan-out queries, up from 21.6% with GPT-5.5, while inline citations fell 12.9%.
key_stats: site: searches: 554 of 729 fan-out queries (76%) for Luna vs 158 of 733 (21.6%) for GPT-5.5
Consulted sources fell 43%, from 6,134 to 3,481; open searches fell from 575 to 175
Inline citations fell 12.9%, from 2,054 to 1,790, across 346 matched prompts

method.sample: 346 matched prompts across six industries, run on both GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Luna (733 vs 729 fan-out queries)
method.data_source: Seer's own prompt runs on ChatGPT; collection method (interface vs API, runs per prompt, prompt list) not disclosed
method.timeframe: Not disclosed. The article says Luna became the default on July 9, 2025, which looks inconsistent with the 2026 publish date.
method.conflict: Seer sells AI search consulting and ends with a sales pitch, but the findings are not tied to one product. The advice to track the full retrieval process does favor its services.
method.caveat: The sample is modest, with one snapshot and no variance or repeat runs. The explanations, such as Luna being "better at finding information", are hypotheses, and the article doesn't say how prompts were chosen or how many are branded vs non-brand.

brief.why_it_matters: If citations dropped after the default model switched, the cause may be the platform, not your tests. Annotate the switch in reporting and track fan-out queries and site: targeting for your domain, not just citations.

briefs.title: Incident details | Google Search Status Dashboard

brief.headline: Google released the September 2026 spam update on 24 Sep 2026 at 09:15 PDT, global and all languages, with rollout taking up to two weeks.
key_stats: Released 24 Sep 2026, 09:15 PDT
Applies globally and to all languages
Rollout may take up to two weeks to complete

method.sample: n/a (official announcement)
method.data_source: n/a (official announcement)
method.timeframe: Rollout began 24 Sep 2026 09:15 PDT; may take up to two weeks to complete
method.conflict: Google does not say which spam policies or tactics are targeted, how many sites are affected, or what recovery requires.
method.caveat: The entry gives only the date, scope and rollout window. It names no targeted spam types, so any diagnosis of a traffic drop is guesswork until Google or the wider industry says more.

brief.why_it_matters: Ranking volatility is likely through early October. Log any traffic changes against the rollout window and avoid big content changes until it finishes. Check your content and link practices against Google's spam policies.

briefs.title: AI Overviews Cut CTR by 23.1% in France

brief.headline: In France, domains with over 20% of queries triggering AI Overviews lost 23.1% median CTR in nine days; the panel median fell 5.7%.
key_stats: Highly exposed domains: CTR -23.1% (raw; -24.8% after control adjustment); 82.2% of them lost CTR
Slope of -0.9 across 963 domains: about one point of CTR lost per point of AI Overview exposure
Full panel median: -5.7% CTR and -8.8% clicks; 48% of domains lost more than 10% of daily clicks, 5% lost more than 50%

method.sample: 963 of the 1,000 highest-click French domains (those with full history); 28 days before vs 9 days after July 22, 2026
method.data_source: Aggregated Google Search Console data; AI Overview rate per domain (share of queries triggering one) from Ahrefs
method.timeframe: Baseline 28 days before July 22, 2026, compared with 9 days after; domain selection based on April–July 2026
method.conflict: Ahrefs sells the Site Explorer tool it recommends for measuring AI Overview exposure, and promotes its AI marketing platform. The finding of a large AI Overview impact does not directly sell the product.
method.caveat: The post-launch window is only 9 days, the panel is limited to top-click domains (not typical B2B SaaS sites), and it is a group comparison, not a controlled test. The control group is the near-unexposed domains, and the −0.9 slope is described by the authors as crude and not a prediction.

brief.why_it_matters: Gives a rough way to size AI Overview risk: check the share of your queries that trigger one, expect similar CTR loss, and track clicks and CTR rather than impressions. The window is short, so treat it as an estimate.

briefs.title: 2026 Blogging Statistics: Blogger Data Shows Trends and Insights Into Blogging

brief.headline: Only 14% of 1,042 content marketers report strong blog results, an all-time low; 92% use AI, and AI use shows no link to strong results.
key_stats: 13.9% report strong results (previously 20–30% for 12 years); 18% don't know if their blog delivers results
92.4% use AI for blogging; AI users and non-users are equally likely to report strong results, but non-users more often report disappointing results
Influencer collaboration beats the benchmark by 2.6x but fell from 25% of marketers in 2017 to 7%; using six or more of eight strategies makes strong results nearly three times as likely

method.sample: 1,042 content marketers responding to a 24-question survey
method.data_source: Orbit Media's annual blogger survey (13th year); self-reported results, correlations between tactics and "strong results"
method.timeframe: 2026 survey wave; trend data back to 2014. Exact fieldwork dates not disclosed
method.conflict: Orbit is a content marketing agency. It sells a book and describes its own program (research, visuals, events) as matching the tactics that correlate with success.
method.caveat: Results are self-reported and correlational. The article attributes the drop to abandoned tactics, but the data cannot show cause. Recruitment method, respondent mix and statistical tests are not described, and "strong results" is undefined.

brief.why_it_matters: Don't expect AI to give you an edge. Keep the labor-heavy tactics (original research, human editing, keyword research, expert collaboration), and judge content by CRM outcomes, not traffic.

briefs.title: LLM Citation Study: 13,184 Citations Across 4 AI Tools | Orbit Media Studios

brief.headline: Across 1,792 query-domain combinations, all four LLMs cited the same domain for the same question only 30 times (1.7%).
key_stats: Only 10% to 30% of domains cited by models also ranked in Google's top 10; exact-URL overlap roughly 1% to 5% for Gemini and ChatGPT
Two runs two days apart: Claude kept 30% of cited URLs, Gemini 38% of domains, Perplexity 65%
Mentioned vs cited: Claude 70% vs 40%, Gemini 72% vs 41%, Perplexity 67% vs 44%, ChatGPT 56% vs 47%

method.sample: 13,184 citations and 1,765 answers from 72 prompts (12-40 per brand) across three brands, run on ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity
method.data_source: Author-built tracker (made with Claude Code) that runs weekly. Google top-10 results pulled for prompts that could be mapped to a keyword. ChatGPT run with web search forced on. Claude run through an agent-with-search setup, not the raw API.
method.timeframe: About 3 months from the start of summer, with data through August 23, 2026
method.conflict: No direct product push. The author sells AI visibility audits and links to his tracker, and one of the three tracked brands is his own site. Another is a client, Semrush.
method.caveat: Only three brands, two of them tiny and one of them Semrush. The author calls the prompt count "directional, not statistical proof". The Claude setup differs from claude.ai, Gemini often gives only the domain, and the Reddit and stability results rest on one or two weekly runs.

brief.why_it_matters: Do not judge AI visibility from one run or one engine. The results support tracking mentions and citations over several weeks. They also suggest that third-party listicles and review sites matter more than Reddit for B2B, but the sample is too small to be sure.

briefs.title: AI Traffic Conversion Rates: New Research from 97 B2B Websites and 29M visits | Orbit Media Studios

brief.headline: Visitors from AI sources are 3x more likely to convert into leads than other organic traffic, but AI is only 0.5% of traffic across 29M visits.
key_stats: AI visitors convert 3x more than other organic sources; per-site median gap is 7x; pattern holds on around two-thirds of sites
ChatGPT converts 2.1% of visitors into leads vs Google Search 0.5%, but Google drives 100x more traffic
140,000 of 29 million visits (0.5%) came from AI sources; AI visitors are also 2x as likely to do low-intent conversions like newsletter signups

method.sample: 97 B2B/lead-gen GA4 accounts, 28.9 million sessions (about 140,000 AI-referred); each site had at least 100 AI sessions
method.data_source: GA4 accounts; AI sessions identified by source/medium pattern matching; key events manually tiered as high-intent, low-intent or excluded
method.timeframe: July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026
method.conflict: Publisher is an agency that sells AI-readiness and content services, and the article ends with a sales pitch. The finding supports the case for optimizing for AI.
method.caveat: Conversion tiering was manual and the authors call it the most judgment-dependent step. Sites need at least 100 AI sessions, and how the accounts were chosen isn't disclosed. AI traffic is undercounted because AI Overviews and AI Mode land in Organic Search and app visits land in Direct. The reasons given for the gap are hypotheses, not tested.

brief.why_it_matters: AI referrals are worth tracking and optimizing for as a high-intent channel, but at 0.5% of traffic and 100x less volume than Google, they don't replace organic search for lead volume.

briefs.title: AI assistants judge your company by its name - Peec AI

brief.headline: On GPT 5.6 Terra, one in twelve brand descriptions described the name's dictionary meaning instead of the company; the effect appears only for brands models don't recognize.
key_stats: Live data: a name scoring one point higher is described 0.07 points more positively (904 single-word brands, 5 assistants)
Lab: 80 matched name pairs, 640 samples per model; Terra showed the largest effect, roughly four times Gemma's; Gemini's estimate was not significant
Semantic takeover: one description in twelve on Terra; well-known brands like Discord, Riot and Slack were unaffected

method.sample: 904 real single-English-word brands across 5 assistants (live); 80 matched fictional name pairs x 4 descriptions = 640 samples per model across 4 models (lab)
method.data_source: Peec AI's own Brand Perception data (live) plus a controlled lab test with web search off; attributes scored against Warriner et al. 2013 valence ratings
method.timeframe: Live data: one observational week, dates not disclosed. Lab dates not disclosed. Article dated Aug 11, 2026.
method.conflict: Yes. Peec AI sells AI search monitoring, and the article ends by pointing to its new Brand Perception feature, which produced the live data.
method.caveat: Real-world effect is small (0.07 points per point), the lab used fictional brands with no web search and only four models, and the "unknown brands only" explanation is the author's interpretation, not tested directly.

brief.why_it_matters: If your SaaS name is a loaded English word and models don't know you yet, check how they describe you; building recognition matters more than renaming.

briefs.title: Brand Visibility | ChatGPT and Google AI Approaches by Industry

brief.headline: BrightEdge found ChatGPT and Google AI Mode diverge most on action-type prompts, from 39% divergence in finance to 62% in healthcare.
key_stats: Healthcare divergence 62%; B2B tech 47%; education 45%; finance 39%
Comparison prompts: both platforms agree (e.g. AWS and Azure for cloud platforms)
Action prompts: ChatGPT names tools (Kubernetes, AWS CLI for deploying); Google links tutorials and Stack Overflow

method.sample: "Thousands of real-world prompts" across finance, healthcare, B2B technology and education; exact count and per-industry split not disclosed
method.data_source: BrightEdge AI Catalyst platform; responses of ChatGPT and Google AI Mode to identical prompts, with brands mentioned and citation patterns extracted
method.timeframe: July 2025
method.conflict: Yes. BrightEdge sells AI Catalyst, and the report ends by pitching it as the "comprehensive solution" for optimizing across both platforms.
method.caveat: "Divergence" is never defined, and prompt selection, counts and the full report are not shown (the full report is gated). The tool-versus-content claim rests on a few hand-picked examples, so the percentages can't be checked.

brief.why_it_matters: For action-oriented queries, ChatGPT may favor product and tool mentions while Google AI Mode favors guides. That is directional support for having both product-led and educational content, not proof.

briefs.title: AI Search Visits Surging in 2025—But Organic Search Remains the Cornerstone of Digital Growth

brief.headline: AI search drives under 1% of referral traffic and near-zero direct conversions, while organic remains the primary driver, despite double-digit monthly growth (Jan–Aug 2025).
key_stats: AI search accounts for less than 1% of referral traffic; organic delivers the majority of conversions
Grok grew 1279% in July from a small base; Claude grew 58% in July and 21% in August
34% of AI citations come from PR and media coverage; nearly 10% from social platforms such as LinkedIn and Reddit

method.sample: "Thousands of queries and top-performing websites, including many Fortune 100 brands". Exact counts not disclosed.
method.data_source: BrightEdge platform data (own tool). Referral, conversion and citation methods not explained on the page.
method.timeframe: January through August 2025
method.conflict: Yes. BrightEdge sells enterprise SEO and AI search tools, and the page promotes its AI Early Detection System and AI Catalyst.
method.caveat: This is a summary page for a gated report. It gives no sample sizes, no conversion figures and no definition of "conversion", and the growth percentages come from very small bases. Claims such as "the efficiency gap is increasing" have no numbers behind them.

brief.why_it_matters: It broadly confirms what we knew: keep investing in SEO fundamentals, treat AI referrals as top-of-funnel, and look at earning citations from media and forums. The evidence is thin, and the page also sells BrightEdge tools.
